episode_title: Anyons caught at trion traps, forcing weak excitons to absorb, and squeezing moiré potentials with pressure

segments.speaker: Ava
segments.text: It's October fifteenth, and the archive dropped about fifty new papers overnight. We're covering ten of them today.

segments.speaker: Leo
segments.text: Top of the list is a theory paper straight out of Imamoglu's own group, trying to explain why anyon binding energies in twisted molybdenum ditelluride came out suspiciously close to the fractional charge ratio. Then we've got a cavity trick that makes a notoriously weak interlayer exciton absorb light as strongly as the bright intralayer one, a pressure cell squeezing the moiré potential in tungsten diselenide on tungsten disulfide, a magnetic proximity story in tungsten diselenide on chromium tri-iodide, and a near-field microscopy look at strain-engineered single photon emitters.

segments.speaker: Ava
segments.text: Let's start with the anyon paper, first in the show notes. Context: a few months back, a photoluminescence experiment in twisted molybdenum ditelluride saw a trapped trion resonance jump abruptly in energy right past the fractional Chern insulator fillings of minus two-thirds and minus three-fifths. They read that jump as an anyon binding to the trion.

segments.speaker: Leo
segments.text: And the number that got everyone's attention was the ratio of those two binding energies, which came out close to five-thirds — exactly the ratio of the fractional charges at those two fillings. That's the kind of number you'd expect if the trion were acting as a broad probe that just counts total charge.

segments.speaker: Ava
segments.text: Except the trion and the anyon are both positively charged, so their long-range Coulomb interaction should be repulsive, not attractive. The experimental explanation was that the binding comes from the neutral, polarizable exciton inside the trion — which would make the interaction short-ranged, not long-ranged. Short-range probes shouldn't care about total charge, they should care about internal structure. So why did the ratio still come out at five-thirds?

segments.speaker: Leo
segments.text: That's the question Adlong and coauthors tackle. They put a static impurity, with tunable sign and tunable range, into a lowest-Landau-level model and look at how quasiholes and quasiparticles from Jain's composite-fermion sequence bind to it, using exact diagonalization and Monte Carlo sampling of trial wavefunctions.

segments.speaker: Ava
segments.text: First surprise: an anyon's internal density profile isn't monotonic. A quasihole has a net electron deficit, but if you map its density shell by shell, there are rings where it actually piles up electrons. Same the other way for a quasiparticle. So a short-range impurity sitting at one particular radius can see the 'wrong' sign of density change entirely.

segments.speaker: Leo
segments.text: Which leads to the second surprise, the one in the title — wrong-sign binding. A quasihole can bind just as happily to an electron-attractive impurity as to an electron-repulsive one, simply by choosing the angular-momentum channel whose density oscillation happens to line up favorably. The sign of the impurity potential alone doesn't tell you whether you're looking at a quasihole or a quasiparticle.

segments.speaker: Ava
segments.text: And yet — here's the punchline — when they compute the binding-energy ratio between the two-thirds and three-fifths states in the contact limit, where the impurity only talks to the single nearest orbital, it still comes out near five-thirds. Even though that regime is exactly where you'd expect charge-counting to break down.

segments.speaker: Leo
segments.text: So the five-thirds in the real experiment doesn't actually prove fractional charge was measured. It's consistent with a long-range probe picking up pure charge, but it's equally consistent with a short-range probe that just happens to land on this coincidence for these two particular fillings. They show the ratio drifts well away from five-thirds at intermediate impurity ranges, or if you look at other points along the Jain sequence.

segments.speaker: Ava
segments.text: What would settle it?

segments.speaker: Leo
segments.text: Measuring more fractions. If future experiments trap anyons at other filling ratios along the Jain sequence and the binding energies keep tracking the charge ratio, that's good evidence for a genuinely long-range or charge-dominated interaction. If they don't, it means the trion is reading off internal anyon structure, which is actually the more interesting outcome scientifically. The authors are upfront that their model is minimal — no Chern-band geometry, no Landau-level mixing, no real trion internal dynamics, and no anyon-anyon interactions at finite doping, all of which matter for a real device.

segments.speaker: Ava
segments.text: Still, it's a nice cautionary tale for anyone reading off microscopic physics from a single number — including whoever ran that original measurement.

segments.speaker: Leo
segments.text: Next up, paper two: interlayer excitons that have been too weak to use properly, finally forced to absorb light.

segments.speaker: Ava
segments.text: The problem is well known to you specifically — in heterobilayer transition metal dichalcogenides, interlayer excitons have the electron and hole in different layers. Great for dipole physics and long-range transport, terrible for optics, because the wavefunction overlap is tiny and the oscillator strength drops two orders of magnitude below the intralayer exciton. Even in homobilayer molybdenum disulfide, where valence-band hybridization gives interlayer excitons some brightness, they only reach about a quarter of the intralayer A exciton's strength.

segments.speaker: Leo
segments.text: Poudyal and coauthors go after this with critical coupling. An exciton's absorption is set by the competition between its radiative decay rate and its nonradiative decay rate; absorption peaks when the two are equal. You can't change the nonradiative rate much, but you can engineer the radiative rate through the Purcell effect, by controlling the local photonic environment with a cavity.

segments.speaker: Ava
segments.text: So they build a transmission-line model, treating each layer of the stack — hBN, the bilayer, more hBN, a gold mirror — as a circuit element, and derive a closed form for the Purcell factor purely from the cavity's reflectivity, with no exciton parameters in it at all. That's the elegant part: you can design the cavity using only the resonance energy, independent of how weak the oscillator is.

segments.speaker: Leo
segments.text: First they characterize bare, cavity-free bilayer molybdenum disulfide: the interlayer exciton's intrinsic oscillator strength is about twenty-six percent of the A exciton's, and both resonances sit far from critical coupling, with the interlayer exciton four times further away.

segments.speaker: Ava
segments.text: Then the open cavity — hBN spacers on a gold mirror, varying thickness to move the bilayer from a field node to an antinode. Across three devices, the Purcell factor spans more than an order of magnitude, and the interlayer exciton's absorption rises from about five percent to forty-eight percent. The A exciton rises too, from twenty-two to ninety-one percent, but by a smaller factor — nine point six times for the interlayer exciton versus four point one times for A.

segments.speaker: Leo
segments.text: Why the asymmetric boost?

segments.speaker: Ava
segments.text: Because the peak-absorption curve as a function of the dimensionless coupling parameter is steep near zero and flattens out as you approach critical coupling. The A exciton is already partway up that curve, so the same Purcell boost buys it less. The weak interlayer exciton is sitting on the steep part, so it gains disproportionately — the cavity preferentially rescues the weak oscillator.

segments.speaker: Leo
segments.text: Then they close the cavity with a second, thin gold mirror on top, making a proper Fabry-Pérot. Now the Purcell factor becomes spectrally selective instead of flat, and they tune it to peak right at the interlayer exciton energy — giving it a Purcell factor two point three times larger than the A exciton's at that same spot. Result: interlayer exciton absorption of eighty-three percent, versus eighty-four percent for the A exciton. Essentially matched, despite four times less intrinsic oscillator strength.

segments.speaker: Ava
segments.text: For spectroscopy of dipolar excitons, correlated states, polaron physics — this means you no longer need differential or photocurrent tricks to even see the interlayer exciton. You could directly track it in a plain reflectance measurement, which opens the door to dynamics and many-body studies that have been bottlenecked by sheer signal weakness.

segments.speaker: Leo
segments.text: On to paper three: pressure as a knob for the moiré potential itself, in twisted tungsten diselenide on tungsten disulfide.

segments.speaker: Ava
segments.text: Li and coauthors put a diamond anvil cell around a dual-gated, nearly sixty-degree, angle-aligned bilayer — so it's untwisted in the usual sense but forms an eight-nanometer moiré pattern — and do cryogenic reflectance and photoluminescence up to three point six gigapascals.

segments.speaker: Leo
segments.text: At ambient pressure they see three moiré intralayer exciton peaks of the tungsten diselenide layer, labeled X-one, X-two, X-three, arising from zero-momentum and moiré-folded finite-momentum states mixed by the periodic potential. As pressure climbs, they diverge wildly: X-one redshifts eighty-five milli-electron-volts and loses spectral weight, X-three redshifts only forty-three milli-electron-volts but gains weight, X-two blueshifts slightly then disappears, and a brand new peak, X-four, switches on above one point eight gigapascals.

segments.speaker: Ava
segments.text: That's a lot of structure for something as simple-sounding as hydrostatic pressure. How do they pin down what's actually changing in the moiré potential?

segments.speaker: Leo
segments.text: They fit a continuum model — the same one used to predict topological exciton bands — where the moiré landscape is written as a six-term Fourier sum with just two free parameters: an amplitude V and a phase Psi. By matching the energy splittings and relative spectral weights of the four peaks at each pressure, they extract how V and Psi evolve. Both increase with pressure, meaning the potential gets both deeper and steeper near its minima.

segments.speaker: Ava
segments.text: And because exciton-band Chern numbers in this model depend on exactly that amplitude-phase combination, plus a valley Zeeman splitting, they can overlay the pressure trajectory onto a Chern-number phase diagram. It crosses from a trivial region into a region with Chern number plus-or-minus-one — a prediction for a pressure-driven topological transition of the exciton band, not yet directly measured, but falling right out of the fit.

segments.speaker: Leo
segments.text: They also look at how pressure reshapes the coupling between these excitons and doped charge. The X-three exciton, previously identified as having charge-transfer character — electron and hole sitting in different moiré pockets — shows a doping-induced redshift that gets strongly suppressed under pressure, while X-one's redshift barely moves. Via an image-charge screening model, they interpret the shrinking redshift as the electron and hole in X-three being squeezed closer together, losing their charge-transfer character and becoming a more ordinary tightly bound exciton.

segments.speaker: Ava
segments.text: Meanwhile the interlayer exciton goes the opposite way: its repulsion energy with a doped electron at filling one goes up from thirty-eight to fifty-three milli-electron-volts under pressure. Deeper moiré confinement traps both the interlayer exciton and the electron more tightly at the same lattice site, boosting their wavefunction overlap and hence their Coulomb repulsion.

segments.speaker: Leo
segments.text: One catch: above about three gigapascals the linewidths broaden badly, which they attribute to the pressure medium solidifying at cryogenic temperature and losing hydrostaticity — so the high-pressure data is noisier, and they flag helium as a better transmitting medium for future work. Still, this is a genuinely continuous knob on the moiré landscape without needing a new device for every twist angle.

segments.speaker: Ava
segments.text: Paper four moves from mechanical tuning to magnetic. Kuhn and coauthors look at monolayer tungsten diselenide sitting directly on trilayer chromium tri-iodide, a layered magnet, and ask whether the usual picture — that proximity magnetism is set by whichever magnetic layer touches the semiconductor — is actually complete.

segments.speaker: Leo
segments.text: Chromium tri-iodide trilayers are antiferromagnetically stacked at zero field by default, but weak interlayer coupling means you can flip individual layers with a magnetic field, and stacking disorder can even give mixed antiferromagnetic-ferromagnetic configurations. They find two spatial domains on the same device: one purely antiferromagnetic, one mixed.

segments.speaker: Ava
segments.text: For the neutral exciton, the story is clean and matches expectations. Its valley splitting — normally around two milli-electron-volts here — flips sign whenever the adjacent chromium tri-iodide layer flips, in both domains. That's the textbook interfacial proximity picture.

segments.speaker: Leo
segments.text: But then they dope the tungsten diselenide with holes using the gate, and look at the positive trion — no negative trion ever appears, consistent with a staggered band alignment that only lets the Fermi level reach into the valence band. In the purely antiferromagnetic domain, the trion is almost entirely in one circular polarization, meaning holes pile up overwhelmingly in one valley.

segments.speaker: Ava
segments.text: In the mixed domain, though, right in the field range where chromium tri-iodide has that partial ferromagnetic layer order, the trion shows up in both polarizations with comparable strength — the valley-selective hole imbalance just isn't there. And once you crank the field high enough to force all three chromium tri-iodide layers parallel, both domains behave identically again.

segments.speaker: Leo
segments.text: So the trion is reading something the neutral exciton can't see.

segments.speaker: Ava
segments.text: Exactly — the valence-band hole population and alignment in tungsten diselenide depend on the magnetic sequence of the whole trilayer, not just the interfacial layer, even though the simple exciton valley splitting only tracks the interface. The authors can't fully pin down the mechanism — could be a modified band alignment, a changed effective splitting, or interlayer charge transfer — and they're honest that they can't disentangle those possibilities from this data alone. But they do rule out static stacking disorder as the sole explanation, since the domain difference vanishes at high field even though the stacking itself shouldn't change.

segments.speaker: Leo
segments.text: Good reminder that charged excitons and neutral excitons aren't interchangeable probes of a magnetic proximity effect — they can disagree.

segments.speaker: Ava
segments.text: Last deep dive, paper five: a direct look at what strain is actually doing at the nanoscale in the two standard recipes people use to make single-photon emitters in monolayer tungsten diselenide — poking it with an AFM tip, or draping it over fabricated pillars.

segments.speaker: Leo
segments.text: The problem with prior work is that people measured strain from topography with an AFM, and inferred the exciton energy shift separately from far-field optics, assuming the two track each other through a simple elasticity model. Roche and coauthors instead use cryogenic scattering-type near-field optical microscopy — an AFM tip under a tunable laser, acting as a nanoscale antenna, letting them measure the exciton resonance and the topography at the same pixel, with about forty-nanometer resolution, at nine kelvin.

segments.speaker: Ava
segments.text: For the indented samples — tungsten diselenide on a deformable PMMA layer, poked in a grid — the elasticity model, taking the measured topography at face value, predicts local strains of ten to forty percent near the indent, which would mean exciton shifts of hundreds of milli-electron-volts.

segments.speaker: Leo
segments.text: What do they actually measure?

segments.speaker: Ava
segments.text: About fifteen milli-electron-volts, and a blueshift, not a redshift — meaning compressive, not tensile, strain dominates right at the rim around each indent. That's completely at odds with the naive model's prediction of a huge tensile redshift.

segments.speaker: Leo
segments.text: Their explanation: the monolayer tears inside the indentation crater under that much tensile stress, relieving most of the strain, while the material pushed outward during plastic flow of the polymer actually compresses the monolayer at the rim. They back this up with high-resolution AFM images showing visible tears around the indent edges, and the sudden disappearance of any resolvable exciton resonance exactly where the slope is steepest.

segments.speaker: Ava
segments.text: So the topography-based strain estimates used in earlier studies were off by more than an order of magnitude, because they assumed the monolayer stays structurally continuous when it doesn't.

segments.speaker: Leo
segments.text: The pillar-draped samples behave differently — tensile strain dominates as expected from simple draping, and the measured shifts, from about 1.76 down to 1.725 electron-volts near a pillar, are in reasonable agreement with the elasticity model this time, since draping doesn't rely on adhesive plastic flow the way indentation does.

segments.speaker: Ava
segments.text: And yet both techniques produce single-photon emitters at similarly high yield. If the actual strain achieved by indentation is so much smaller than assumed, simple strain-confinement can't be the whole story for why these emitters turn on.

segments.speaker: Leo
segments.text: Their takeaway is that the tears themselves — dangling bonds, edge defect states — are plausibly doing a lot of the work in localizing emission, alongside whatever strain is genuinely present. It's a nice methods result for anyone doing strain or defect engineering in two-dimensional materials: if you care about microscopic strain, you need a local optical probe, not just an AFM height map and a textbook elasticity formula.

segments.speaker: Ava
segments.text: Quick ones now. Paper six, Deng and coauthors argue that the superconductivity recently found in rhombohedral multilayer graphene and in twisted bilayer tungsten diselenide might share a common origin — a metallic Wigner crystal phase in the graphene, stabilized by a W-shaped band dispersion, whose length scale happens to match the moiré period of the twisted dichalcogenide.

segments.speaker: Leo
segments.text: They build an effective triangular-lattice model from this picture and find it breaks three-fold rotation symmetry in part of the phase diagram — a theoretical proposal more than a direct experimental claim, but a nice unifying angle on two unrelated-looking superconductors.

segments.speaker: Ava
segments.text: Paper seven: Graham, Abouelkomsan and Fu throw a neural-network variational wavefunction at the long-standing problem of which non-Abelian state sits at filling three-halves, this time including every electron and every Landau level rather than projecting to the lowest one.

segments.speaker: Leo
segments.text: Without any hint about what to expect, the network discovers a degenerate ground-state manifold whose entanglement structure matches anyons with quantum dimension root-two — the Ising-type signature everyone's been chasing — and comparing overlaps, they find realistic Landau-level mixing favors the anti-Pfaffian state over its rivals.

segments.speaker: Ava
segments.text: Paper eight: Sun, Palle and coauthors report tunneling spectroscopy evidence for a nodal nematic superconducting state in magic-angle twisted trilayer graphene. The zero-bias tunneling conductance shows a two-fold anisotropy under in-plane field that tracks the superconducting dome and rotates its axis by up to ninety degrees as density changes.

segments.speaker: Leo
segments.text: That's a rotational symmetry breaking that seems to be intrinsic to the pairing itself, not inherited from a pre-existing nematic normal state — one of the few clean examples of that distinction being made experimentally.

segments.speaker: Ava
segments.text: Paper nine, more theoretical: Kattan and Sipe use a field-theory treatment of Chern insulators to show their optical activity — Faraday and Kerr rotation — survives even at long wavelength, unlike ordinary chiral materials where it's a finite-wavelength effect. Applied to a thin film of manganese bismuth telluride in its Chern phase, the predicted rotations are many orders of magnitude larger than topologically trivial optically active materials of similar thickness.

segments.speaker: Leo
segments.text: And finally paper ten, Spasic-Mlacak and Cooper, asking which local Hamiltonians can host exactly flat Chern bands beyond the lowest-Landau-level analogy — they work out the conditions for Bernal bilayer graphene with nonzero flux and extend the construction to multi-orbital chains. Pretty formal, but it's useful groundwork for anyone designing flat-band models by hand rather than hunting for them in real materials.

segments.speaker: Ava
segments.text: That's today's set — an anyon paper questioning its own headline number, a cavity trick rescuing a weak exciton, and pressure as a new dial on moiré physics.

segments.speaker: Leo
segments.text: Back tomorrow with whatever the archive throws up next.

picks.title: Anyons at impurities: Fractional charge measurement and "wrong sign" binding
picks.abstract: Recent photoluminescence experiments in twisted MoTe2 have reported signatures of anyons binding to trapped trions. The measured binding energies near the fractional Chern insulators at fillings of \nu=-2/3 and -3/5 have a ratio close to the fractional-charge ratio 5/3, even though such scaling is not generally guaranteed for the expected short-range trion-anyon interaction. We model the trapped trion as a fixed impurity, and investigate anyon-impurity binding using a lowest-Landau-level model with exact diagonalization and Jain wavefunctions. Surprisingly, we find that the anyon-impurity binding energy ratio between \nu=-2/3 and -3/5 is close to 5/3 for either short- or long-ranged impurity-electron interactions. However, the ratio departs strongly from the charge ratio at intermediate ranges or different Jain states. Remarkably, we also uncover "wrong-sign" binding, whereby both quasiholes and quasiparticles can bind to either sign of a short-range impurity potential by selecting orbital channels with favorable local density oscillations. Our findings show that localized excitons or trions can be used to probe the internal density profile of anyons.
picks.why: Direct theoretical follow-up on twisted MoTe2 anyon-trion binding experiments from Imamoglu's own group, revealing surprising 'wrong-sign' binding and probing anyon internal structure via optically trapped excitons/trions.

picks.title: Making Weak Interlayer Excitons Absorb: Manipulating the Effective Oscillator Strength via Purcell Engineering of Critical Coupling
picks.abstract: Interlayer excitons (IXs) in transition metal dichalcogenide bilayers possess unique dipolar properties, providing a path for exploring correlated many-body phases, electrically tunable dipole-dipole interactions, and long-range exciton transport. However, the large electron-hole separation underlying their dipolar character also results in a significantly reduced oscillator strength, limiting their direct optical interaction with light, and thus the direct probing of their dynamics and many-body interactions. Here, we show that by using Purcell engineering of critical coupling, a weak interlayer transition can absorb as strongly as the dominant intralayer transition, despite its much smaller intrinsic oscillator strength. Using this approach, in an open cavity architecture we demonstrate an order of magnitude IX absorption modulation in bilayer and trilayer MoS2, with doubling of the IX to A-exciton interaction strength weight from ~23% to ~53%. Furthermore, we demonstrate that in a tailored closed cavity architecture, the IX enhancement can reach beyond an order of magnitude, from ~5% to ~83% excitonic absorption, enabling IX absorption similar to intralayer excitons. An analytical description of the interaction is obtained via a closed-form transmission-line model which separates the excitonic and photonic contributions to the optical response, revealing how cavity architecture can be designed towards critical coupling. Our findings establish Purcell engineering of critical coupling as a general route to controlling and enhancing weak excitonic transitions.
picks.why: Demonstrates Purcell engineering of cavity critical coupling to boost weak interlayer exciton absorption by an order of magnitude, a powerful new technique for probing dipolar excitons in TMD bilayers.

picks.title: Pressure engineering of the excitonic moiré-potential landscape and exciton-charge interplay in semiconductor moiré superlattices
picks.abstract: Semiconductor moiré superlattices, owing to strongly bound excitons and pronounced electronic correlation, have emerged as an intriguing solid platform for exploring correlated bosonic phenomena, where the moiré potential landscape plays a central role. Hydrostatic pressure allows continuous, in-situ tuning of this landscape, but remains underexplored because of experimental challenges. Here we integrate a diamond anvil pressure cell with high quality dual gated WSe2/WS2 twisted bilayers and perform cryogenic optical spectroscopy. We observe distinct pressure evolutions of moiré intralayer excitons, which reveal drastic modulation of the excitonic moiré-potential landscape captured by a continuum model and suggest the capability of engineering the exciton-band topology. Moreover, we demonstrate efficient pressure control over the interplay between charges and both intralayer and interlayer excitons: the intralayer charge-transfer exciton becomes less sensitive to doping, likely due to reduced charge-transfer character; in contrast, the interlayer exciton exhibits enhanced exciton-charge repulsion. Our results establish hydrostatic pressure as a powerful tuning knob for engineering bosonic quasiparticles and Bose-Fermi interactions in moiré materials.
picks.why: Combines diamond anvil pressure cells with dual-gated twisted WSe2/WS2 optical spectroscopy to continuously tune the moiré potential landscape and exciton-charge interactions, a novel knob for moiré exciton physics.

picks.title: Magnetic proximity beyond the interface: Layer-sequence-dependent exchange in WSe2/CrI3 heterostructures
picks.abstract: Magnetic proximity effects in transition metal dichalcogenide (TMD)/2D-magnet heterostructures are often described in terms of the magnetization of the interfacial magnetic layer. Here, we show that this picture is sufficient to describe the neutral-exciton valley splitting of the TMD, but incomplete for its hole-doped electronic structure. We study a gate-tunable van der Waals heterostructure composed of monolayer WSe2 in direct contact with trilayer CrI3. By combining spatially and helicity-resolved reflection-contrast spectroscopy with magnetic circular dichroism, we identify two distinct magnetic domains in the trilayer CrI3: one with purely antiferromagnetic interlayer coupling and one with a mixed antiferromagnetic (AFM)/ferromagnetic~(FM) coupling. In both domains, the sign of the neutral-exciton valley splitting of WSe2 switches with the magnetization reversal of the adjacent CrI3 layer. In contrast, helicity-resolved positive-trion spectroscopy of WSe2 reveals a qualitatively different response. While the AFM domain shows a strongly helicity-selective trion resonance, the mixed AFM/FM domain exhibits trion resonances in both helicities. This behavior disappears when all CrI3 layers are aligned in a parallel magnetization direction. Our results demonstrate that charged excitons are sensitive to the full layer-resolved magnetic sequence of the adjacent 2D-magnet, revealing magnetic proximity beyond the interface.
picks.why: Helicity-resolved spectroscopy of WSe2/CrI3 heterostructures shows that trion valley physics is sensitive to the full layer-resolved magnetic order of the adjacent 2D magnet, not just the interfacial layer, refining the magnetic proximity picture central to TMD valleytronics.

picks.title: Nanoscale Mapping of Strain-engineered Excitons in Monolayer WSe2
picks.abstract: Excitons in monolayer transition metal dichalcogenides (TMDs) are highly sensitive to external stimuli, allowing control of resonance energies and lifetimes through electric and magnetic fields, heterostructures, moire potentials and mechanical strain. Observations of single-photon emission (SPE) near sample edges, wrinkles, and strained nanobubbles have motivated strain-engineering aimed at realizing localized emitters in 2D materials. The origin of these emitters remains unclear and prior studies have relied on far-field spectroscopy with strain profiles inferred separately through topography, limiting direct correlation between local strain and excitonic response. We directly probe strain-modified excitonic spectra in monolayer WSe2 using cryogenic scattering-type scanning near-field optical microscopy (s-SNOM). We compare two strain-engineering techniques, nano-indentation and patterned substrates, used to produce SPEs. At 9 K, we spatially resolve exciton resonance shifts with sub-diffraction limit resolution, simultaneously measuring near-field optical response and topography. We observe that strain transferred from nano-indentation into a deformable polymer substrate differs from that produced by draping TMDs over patterned dielectric pillars. Adhesion and tearing during plastic deformation drive a compressive exciton blueshift, while draping produces dominant tensile strain. Comparing the strain model results to the experimentally observed energy shifts shows that the nano-indentation strain is over an order of magnitude smaller than previously inferred, due to puncturing of the fragile monolayer, whereas pillar-strained devices remain intact under more modest strain. These differences suggest SPE arises from complex, strain-mediated interactions rather than simple confinement potentials, establishing s-SNOM as a powerful probe of quantum emission in strained 2D materials.
picks.why: Cryogenic s-SNOM nanoscale mapping directly correlates strain and exciton energy shifts in monolayer WSe2, resolving the long-standing ambiguity about the origin of strain-induced single-photon emitters.

picks.title: Metallic electron crystals in rhombohedral graphene as a bridge to twisted WSe2
picks.abstract: Superconducting phases have recently been discovered both in twisted bilayers of transition metal dichalcogenide WSe2 (tWSe2) and in rhombohedral multilayer graphene (RMG). While both have generated extensive interest, they appear to be driven by qualitatively different physics. Here, we propose a unified picture in which the superconductivity in RMG arises from a strongly correlated metallic state with a spatial length scale that is compatible with the moiré length scale of tWSe2. Central to this mechanism is a Wigner crystal phase in RMG that is metallic, driven by a "W"-shaped dispersion in the flat part of the underlying graphene band structure. We demonstrate this effect through calculations of Wigner crystal states in pentalayer RMG, focusing on dilute electrons in the quarter-metal regime relevant to experiment. In a region of the phase diagram we find the Wigner crystal breaks three-fold rotation symmetry, which guides our construction of a t-V model on a triangular lattice as an effective description of the low-energy electronic physics. This construction suggests a surprisingly similar low-energy description of RMG and tWSe2. Broader implications for superconductivity in dilute carrier systems are also discussed.
picks.why: Proposes a unifying Wigner-crystal mechanism linking superconductivity in rhombohedral graphene to the moiré physics of twisted WSe2, directly bridging two systems in the listener's core interests.

picks.title: Non-Abelian quantum Hall states at strong Landau level mixing: finding anyons with first-principles AI
picks.abstract: Non-Abelian anyons, strange particles forming the basis of fault-tolerant topological quantum computing, are predicted to emerge in fractional quantum Hall states at even-denominator filling factors. Identifying which topological order is realized has proven to be a challenging problem that requires an accurate, non-perturbative treatment of realistic Landau level mixing, which has so far been missing from theoretical studies. Here we present the first complete solution of non-Abelian quantum Hall problem that includes all electrons and all Landau levels, for spin-polarized electrons at filling factor \nu = 3/2. We develop a momentum-resolved neural-network variational wave function, optimized solely on the microscopic Hamiltonian, which gives direct access to the topologically degenerate ground states. Without any physics input about the expected outcome, it discovers a degenerate ground-state manifold whose entanglement reveals anyons with quantum dimension \sqrt2, the hallmark of Ising-type non-Abelian order. By directly computing the overlap with trial wave functions, we further show that Landau level mixing favors the anti-Pfaffian over other candidate states. Our results demonstrate the power of neural-network wave functions in finding and characterizing non-Abelian anyons from first principles, in regimes of strong Landau level mixing, relevant to many recent experiments.
picks.why: First-principles neural-network variational wavefunctions identify Ising-type non-Abelian anyons at nu=3/2 with full Landau-level mixing, a significant advance for fractional quantum Hall anyon physics.

picks.title: Nodal nematic superconductivity in moiré graphene
picks.abstract: Unconventional superconductivity can emerge in various forms in strongly correlated systems. Historically, the most extensively studied examples include nodal and triplet pairing, which were experimentally detected in cuprates and superfluid helium-3, respectively. Beyond these canonical cases, there are also nematic superconductors, in which the rotational symmetry of the lattice is broken in the superconducting state. While there are several examples of nematic superconductors whose pairing emerges inside a preexisting nematic normal state, experimental evidence for superconducting states that intrinsically break rotational symmetry on their own has been exceedingly scarce. Here, we report the experimental realization and identification of an intrinsic multi-component nodal nematic superconducting state in magic-angle twisted trilayer graphene (MATTG). By integrating tunneling spectroscopy with quantum transport measurements, we directly probe the symmetry of low-energy superconducting quasiparticles. Deep inside the superconducting state, we observe a pronounced two-fold anisotropy in the zero-bias tunneling conductance under an in-plane magnetic field, which is strongly suppressed together with superconductivity as the temperature or perpendicular magnetic field is increased. Remarkably, the major axis of anisotropy rotates by up to 90\circ across the superconducting dome, indicating an intrinsic, field- and density-tunable symmetry of the low-energy excitations. These behaviors imply a nodal superconducting state in MATTG that spontaneously breaks the six-fold rotational symmetry of the moiré superlattice. Our results establish moiré graphene as a versatile platform for realizing and interrogating nodal nematic superconductivity, opening a new avenue for exploring unconventional symmetry-breaking superconducting states in two-dimensional materials.
picks.why: Tunneling and transport evidence for an intrinsic nodal nematic superconducting state in magic-angle twisted trilayer graphene that spontaneously breaks moiré lattice rotational symmetry.

picks.title: Chern insulator optics
picks.abstract: Chern insulators have optical properties that are strikingly different than ordinary chiral media. Unlike the natural optical activity of the latter, which is a finite-wavelength effect arising from spatial dispersion, the optical activity of a Chern insulator is already present in the long-wavelength limit, and exhibits a striking directional asymmetry in the propagation of circularly polarized light. We study this unnatural optical activity using a recently developed field theory for Chern insulators. For bulk Chern insulators, we derive the normal-incidence transmission and reflection coefficients of multilayer structures, identify the associated Faraday and Kerr angles, and show that these optical rotations provide a direct optical signature of topology at low frequencies. We also show that an interface between bulk Chern insulators can act as a kind of mirror, completely reflecting light at normal incidence when the Chern invariants have opposite signs. Moving to a more realistic model of a two-dimensional current sheet, we study the Faraday and Kerr effects in a thin film of MnBi2Te4 in its Chern insulator phase. The predicted rotations are many orders of magnitude larger than those of optically active media of comparable thickness that are topologically trivial.
picks.why: Develops a field theory for the unusual long-wavelength optical activity and giant Faraday/Kerr rotations of Chern insulators like MnBi2Te4, connecting topology to directly measurable optics.

picks.title: Designing Hamiltonians with Exactly Flat Higher-Vortexable Bands
picks.abstract: The zero modes of the Aharonov-Casher Hamiltonian form an exactly flat, vortexable Chern band in any nonuniform magnetic field, analogous to the lowest Landau level. We ask which local Hamiltonians host exactly flat higher-vortexable bands. For a scalar Hamiltonian, an exactly flat first-vortexable band requires a mass proportional to the local field; the Dirac analogue has the same structure. For periodic Bernal bilayer graphene with nonzero mean flux, the exact zero-mode pair is genuinely first-vortexable if and only if the interlayer hopping has nonzero mean; zero-mean hopping instead gives a decomposable pair. Multiorbital models yield exact higher-vortexable chains to arbitrary order, while remaining first order in momentum.
picks.why: Extends the flat-band/vortexable-band framework (relevant to moiré flat-band physics) to higher-order analogues, including explicit conditions in Bernal bilayer graphene.
